title: The Complete Indonesia Travel Guide
subtitle: Volcanoes, temples, reefs and dragons across the world's largest archipelago
summary: How to plan an Indonesia trip: which islands to combine, how to get between them, when to go for dry-season weather, what it costs, and a practical ten-day itinerary.

sections.title: How Indonesia divides
body: Indonesia divides into distinct island regions, each with its own character — treating the whole archipelago as one trip is the most common planning mistake.
**Bali.** [[ubud|Ubud]] inland and [[seminyak-kuta|Seminyak and Kuta]] on the coast — temples, rice terraces, surf and the country's most developed tourist infrastructure.

**Java.** [[yogyakarta-borobudur|Yogyakarta and Borobudur]] for ancient temples, [[bromo-tengger-semeru|Mount Bromo]] for volcanic drama, and the capital [[jakarta|Jakarta]] and nearby [[bandung|Bandung]] for city life.
**The eastern islands.** [[komodo-flores|Komodo and Flores]] for wild dragons and island-hopping, and [[raja-ampat|Raja Ampat]] further east for the richest reefs on Earth.

**Beyond Java and Bali.** [[lombok-gili-islands|Lombok and the Gili Islands]] for a quieter beach alternative to Bali, and [[lake-toba-sumatra|Lake Toba]] in Sumatra for volcanic lake scenery and Batak culture.
sections.note: Most first-time visitors combine Bali with one other region — Java or Komodo — rather than attempting the whole archipelago in one trip.

list.title: If this is your first trip
list.text: [[ubud|Ubud]] and [[seminyak-kuta|Seminyak or Kuta]], the classic short Bali route and the most popular for a reason.

list.title: If you want ancient temples and volcanoes
list.text: Add [[yogyakarta-borobudur|Yogyakarta and Borobudur]] and [[bromo-tengger-semeru|Mount Bromo]] to a Bali base for real cultural and geological depth.

list.title: If you want wild Komodo dragons
list.text: [[komodo-flores|Komodo and Flores]], the only place on Earth to see these giant lizards in the wild.

list.title: If you want the best diving on Earth
list.text: [[raja-ampat|Raja Ampat]], worth the extra flights for marine biodiversity nowhere else can match.

list.title: If you want Bali's beaches without the crowds
list.text: [[lombok-gili-islands|Lombok and the Gili Islands]], quieter and slower-paced just next door.

list.title: If you want city life and highland scenery
list.text: [[jakarta|Jakarta]] and [[bandung|Bandung]] on Java, or [[lake-toba-sumatra|Lake Toba]] in Sumatra for a different side of Indonesia.

sections.title: Getting around: flights, ferries and one common mistake
body: Indonesia's islands require real planning to connect — this isn't a country where you can casually drive between regions.
**Fly between islands, don't try to drive or ferry everywhere.** Domestic flights are affordable and by far the most time-efficient way to connect Bali, Java and the eastern islands.
**Don't underestimate island-hopping logistics.** A route that looks like a short hop on a map can mean a flight plus a boat plus a long drive — build in buffer days.
**Use Gojek or Grab in cities and larger towns.** The easiest, most transparent way to get around without haggling over fares.
**Book Komodo and Raja Ampat trips well ahead in dry season.** Liveaboards and dive trips sell out months ahead in the July–August peak.
**Check volcanic activity advisories before Bromo or Ijen treks.** Access closes at short notice when activity increases.
sections.note: Build at least one buffer day into any itinerary involving Komodo or Raja Ampat — boats and small-plane connections there are more weather-dependent than mainland transport.

sections.title: When to go
body: Indonesia's equatorial climate means the dry-versus-wet season split matters more than temperature, which stays warm nearly year-round. Dry season, roughly **April to October**, is the most reliable window.
**Dry season (April–October)** brings the most reliable weather for Bromo treks, Komodo boat trips and Raja Ampat diving — also the busiest and most expensive season, especially July and August.
**Shoulder months**, April and October specifically, offer a good balance of dry-season weather and thinner crowds.

**Wet season (November–March)** still works well for Bali and Java, with short, heavy daily downpours rather than constant rain, though rougher seas can disrupt boat-dependent trips to Komodo or Raja Ampat.
**Ramadan**, which shifts each year, sees shorter daytime hours at some restaurants in Muslim-majority Java, though Bali and most tourist infrastructure carry on largely as normal.
sections.note: Book Komodo liveaboards and Raja Ampat dive resorts many months ahead for July–August — this is the busiest, most tightly booked window of the year.

list.title: One week: Bali alone
list.text: [[ubud|Ubud]] and [[seminyak-kuta|Seminyak or Kuta]], the most popular short Indonesia itinerary and complete enough on its own.
list.tip: Split your time roughly evenly between Ubud's culture and the coast's beaches for the best balance.

list.title: Ten days: Bali and Java
list.text: The itinerary on the [[c:indonesia|Indonesia country page]]: [[seminyak-kuta|Seminyak]], [[ubud|Ubud]], [[yogyakarta-borobudur|Yogyakarta and Borobudur]], and [[bromo-tengger-semeru|Mount Bromo]]. A rich first look at both islands.
list.tip: Book the Bali-to-Yogyakarta flight and Bromo jeep tour ahead — both get busy in peak season.

list.title: Two weeks: add Komodo
list.text: Extend the ten-day route with [[komodo-flores|Komodo National Park]] for wild dragons and island-hopping by boat, flying in via Labuan Bajo.
list.tip: A two or three-night liveaboard covers more of Komodo's islands than day trips alone.

list.title: A Raja Ampat add-on for a second trip
list.text: [[raja-ampat|Raja Ampat]] by liveaboard or dive resort, one of the most biodiverse reef systems anywhere on Earth.
list.tip: Fly via Sorong, and book dive trips several months ahead for dry-season visibility.

faq.q: How many days do you need in Indonesia?
faq.a: Ten to fourteen days covers Bali and Java at a reasonable pace, which is the itinerary in this guide. Five to seven days is enough for Bali alone, and still worthwhile on its own.

faq.q: Is it easy to island-hop in Indonesia?
faq.a: Yes, with some planning — domestic flights and ferries connect the main islands reliably, though eastern Indonesia (Komodo, Raja Ampat) needs more buffer time than Bali or Java.

faq.q: Do you need to speak Indonesian?
faq.a: Not really, in tourist areas — English is widely spoken in Bali and major cities, though a few basic Indonesian phrases go a long way elsewhere.

faq.q: When should I visit for diving in Raja Ampat?
faq.a: Roughly October to April for the calmest seas and best visibility, though the peak dry-season window (October–April) can vary by specific dive site — check with operators directly.
